criterion_notes.c1: No. Although the survey collected descriptive background attributes on respondents' household daytime sanitation location, defecation facility type, and toilet sharing (Table 1, p. 12), the study does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access; its sole objective is the psychometric validation of 16 scales measuring women's sanitation-related empowerment.
criterion_notes.c2: No under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, although the scale suite title contains the sociological term 'Institutional Structures' from van Eerdewijk et al.'s empowerment framework, those structures are operationalized solely as social 'Norms' (21 items) and interpersonal/social 'Relations' (11 items) scales undergoing psychometric testing, rather than any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance factor governing service access (and even if 'Institutional Structures' were treated generously under the plain wording, plain_criterion2_decision remains 'exclude' because C1 and C4 fail). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, no rule-type mechanism directly governing service access—such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure—is examined.
criterion_notes.c3: Yes. The study analyzes primary quantitative survey data collected from 5,586 adult women across eight cities in five countries (with a 2-month retest subsample of 257 women in two cities) using exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, multi-group invariance testing, composite reliability, and validity analyses.
criterion_notes.c4: No. All reported outcomes in the study are psychometric measurement properties of the 16 ARISE empowerment scales (factor loadings, RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, TLI, omega internal consistency, intraclass correlation coefficients for test-retest reliability, cross-country and longitudinal measurement invariance, and construct/criterion/known-groups validity indicators). It reports no outcome measuring water or sanitation access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: No. While the study population (adult women, individual unit of analysis) and psychometric validation design (cross-sectional survey with a test-retest subsample) are clearly reported, it is a scale-validation study with no substantive exposure variable and no service-access outcome.
criterion_notes.c6: Yes. The full text is published in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: The objective of the study presented here was, therefore, to further evaluate the reliability, validity, and measurement properties of the ARISE scales using data collected from women in eight cities: Meherpur and Saidpur, Bangladesh; Narsapur, Warangal, and Tiruchirappalli, India; Dakar, Senegal; Kampala, Uganda; and Lusaka, Zambia.
types of resources that can contribute to agency (e.g., health, time), and aspects of institutional structures that shape and condition the realization of choice (e.g., norms, relations) [2].

The survey included scales to measure the 16 sub-domains of sanitation-related empowerment, 11 of which included optional menstruation-specific sub-scales for women who experienced a menstrual period in the previous 12 months, and indices to assess women’s direct experiences related to six sub-domains of empowerment [33].

We evaluated the psychometric properties and validity of the ARISE scales among women in eight cities across five countries and found all 16 scales to have clear dimensionality, as demonstrated through EFA and CFA, overall acceptable internal consistency (reliability), and evidence of multiple forms of validity.
Finally, intervention studies should assess the relationship between urban sanitation, sub-domains of women’s empowerment, and health and well-being outcomes for women.

raw_response.outcome: Psychometric properties of the 16 ARISE women's sanitation-related empowerment scales (EFA/CFA dimensionality and model fit, internal consistency omega, test-retest ICCs, cross-country and longitudinal measurement invariance, and construct/criterion/known-groups validity)
raw_response.population_and_sample: 5,586 adult women aged 18 years or older (individual unit of analysis) sampled from urban households across eight cities: Meherpur (N=720) and Saidpur (N=730), Bangladesh; Narsapur (N=721), Tiruchirappalli (N=563), and Warangal (N=704), India; Dakar, Senegal (N=720); Kampala, Uganda (N=713); and Lusaka, Zambia (N=715), including a 2-month test-retest subsample of 257 women in Dakar (N=125) and Lusaka (N=132)
raw_response.rationale: Exclude (E01: Wrong topic; also fails C2/E03 and C4/E04). This paper is a psychometric instrument evaluation of the 16 Agency, Resources, and Institutional Structures for Sanitation-related Empowerment (ARISE) survey scales among 5,586 women in eight Asian and African cities. It does not examine determinants of water or sanitation service access (C1), does not evaluate any legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance factor under either the plain wording or the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 ('Institutional Structures' in ARISE refers solely to social Norms and interpersonal Relations scale items) (C2), and reports only psychometric properties (factor fit, omega reliability, test-retest ICCs, measurement invariance, and scale validity) rather than any water or sanitation service-access outcome (C4).
raw_response.study_design: Cross-sectional multi-city psychometric validation survey with cognitive interviews and a two-month test-retest subsample
